title: Lab 1: FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text: In this lab, we leveraged the FPGA aboard the MicroP’s Dev Board (which was soldered and constructed per instructions on the E155 site). The FPGA was designed logically to illuminate two LEDs (also present on the Dev Board) following AND or XOR logic from a 4-input DIP switch. Second, a third LED on the Dev Board was instructed to blink at 2.4 Hz. This was done using a clock divider and the 48 MHz high speed oscillator on the board. Finally, the 4-input DIP switch was also logically connected to a 7-segment display such that the binary input would display the corresponding hexadecimal digit on the display. This lab took a total of 16 hours.

title: Lab 1: FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text:
Design and Testing Methodology
The first logic to approach was the 2 LEDs following simple gate logic. To do this, I used assign statements corresponding to the pins and the gate logic. For the testing methodology, a testbench was made and simulated that would confirm all possible outputs of the logic were properly observed and the LEDs illuminated as expected. This same testbench was also used to confirm module connections occured and the on-board high-speed oscillator (HSOSC) from the iCE40 UltraPlus primitive library was generating a clock signal at 48 MHz.






NoteSimple LED Gate Logic





assign led[0] = s[1] ^ s[0]; //XOR logic for one LED
assign led[1] = s[3] & s[2]; //AND logic for another LED



On the note of the high-speed oscillator, the int_osc generated by the top-level module was the used in a blinker submodule as a clock input. With this input, a clock divider was created to convert 48 MHz to 2.4 Hz. This was done with a counter that reset when the counter reached 10,000,000. By parameterizing the MAX count, we can then use an easier testing module. The module also includes “reset” and “en” input logic so after testing that with proper LED output, we generate a different clock and parameterize so MAX count is 3 in the testbench. This allows us to see that when MAX count is reached, the counter does reset to 0 and the LED does toggle.






NoteBlinking Logic





logic [WIDTH-1:0] counter = 1'b0; //initial state of counter

// Simple clock divider
always_ff @(posedge int_osc)
    begin
        if (counter >= MAX) //The reason we want it to count up to this is because a 24 MHz clock divided by the trigger (10000000) as seen here to achieve 2.4 Hz
            begin
            counter <= 0;
            fpga_blink_out <= ~fpga_blink_out;
            end
        else if (!reset)
            begin
                counter <= 0;
                fpga_blink_out <= 0;
            end
        else begin
            if (en) counter <= counter + 1;
        end
    end



Finally, the design logic for the seven segment display was implemented using an always_comb block with cases covering every 4-bit binary input and lighting up the relevant segments to create the hexadecimal digit. The seven bit output simply followings A-G segments as defined in the E155 logic to toggle segments. To test this, I covered all 16 cases and asserted the logical outputs and it passed with flying colors! (get it?)






NoteSeven Segment Combinational Logic





always_comb
    begin
        case(s)
            4'b0000: seg = 7'b0000001; //0
            4'b0001: seg = 7'b1001111; //1
            4'b0010: seg = 7'b0010010; //2
            4'b0011: seg = 7'b0000110; //3
            4'b0100: seg = 7'b1001100; //4
            4'b0101: seg = 7'b0100100; //5
            4'b0110: seg = 7'b0100000; //6
            4'b0111: seg = 7'b0001111; //7
            4'b1000: seg = 7'b0000000; //8
            4'b1001: seg = 7'b0000100; //9
            4'b1010: seg = 7'b0001000; //A
            4'b1011: seg = 7'b1100000; //B
            4'b1100: seg = 7'b0110001; //C
            4'b1101: seg = 7'b1000010; //D
            4'b1110: seg = 7'b0110000; //E
            4'b1111: seg = 7'b0111000; //F
            default: seg = 7'b1111111; //default case
        endcase
    end

title: Digital Audio
text:
In this lab, we leveraged the MCU aboard the MicroP’s Dev Board, particularly the STM32L4xx model. Utilizing this, we’re able to control the timer logic to function like a counter in order to trigger an output at a certain frequency. This is done via the TIM2 register built into the MCU as well as initiating the GPIO B pins to output a signal that powers a speaker at the desired frequency. With all these puzzle pieces, we can have the speaker play an array of notes and make a tune.
I spent approximately 14 hours in this lab all together including familiarizing myself with the idea and a whole lot of debugging

Multiplexed Seven Segment Display
text:
In this lab, we built upon the foundation of a single seven segment display leveraged the FPGA aboard the MicroP’s Dev Board to branch out to a dual seven segment display which was integrated using multiplexing logic to properly select a DIP switch as an input the continuously flash the 2 hex digits of the display fast enough to be undetectable to the human eye. The decoding module and counter module are identical to Lab 1 save for a new top-level test bench that makes use of the parameterized counter to flash and assign logic such that the right DIP switch and digit (i.e. common anode on the dual seven segment display) is selected. The multiplexing logic allows us to control 2 digits with just 9 pins and utilizing the counter module, we aim for the internal 48 MHz clock to be divided by ~18’b0 resulting in a clock at ~90 Hz (due to toggling) which is indeed sufficient. Additionally, this lab also included building a scanning module such that a scanning signal be displayed at ~2 Hz on internal LEDs when buttons on a keypad are pressed. The idea is that each row runs at a slightly different offset clock cycle and pressing all 4 columns in conjunction results in a synchronized blinking. Furthermore, the designs of both took advantage of the physics for PNP and NPN transistors as to not drain more than 8 mA for the FPGA pins but get sufficient current draw.
I spent approximately 15 hours in this lab all together including familiarizing myself with the idea and a whole lot of debugging

title: Keypad Scanner
text:
With a few edits to the hardware from Lab 2, we can use the multiplexed display logic and row scanning on the keypad in order to reliably receive inputs from said keypad and display. Specifically, this lab aims to provide functionality to the keypad such that the display records the last two buttons hit on the keypad. In order to achieve this, a FSM reading inputs (to handle presses, lack of press, and multiple presses) was used in tandem with a register that would shift the last digit to the second display. Naturally, other modules in software are required to handle synchronization and debouncing on the keypad. This lab was an immensely thought provoking one and required a clever manipulation and communication between modules.

title: Keypad Scanner
text:
Block Diagram
{#fig-block-diagram} The block diagram in ?@fig-block-diagram demonstrates the overall architecture of the design. The top-level module lab2_ea includes three submodules: the winker/counter which is paramterized for displaying a range of frequencies to the top module or scanner (winker), the scanner which cycles between which bit of the [3:0] row output vector (fed into the keypad) is HIGH (scanner), and the 7-segment display logic module (decoder) Additionally, HS_OSC is also leveraged for an internal 48 MHz clock.Schematic{#fig-schematic}?@fig-schematic shows the electical layout of the design. Because driving every segment at 10 mA is strenuous (especially if we consider a case where both digits display 8), 150 \(\Omega\) was the appropriate value per the equation where \(R_{seg} = (3.3V-2)/10mA\) making 150 our ideal choice. Additionally, the transistors and the resistor values associated with the keypad scanner were also paramount. First, to explain, the display was multiplexed by having 2 independent 2N3906 PNP transistors control a common anode of each digit respectively (specifically the Collector pin of the transistor). These transistors are configured such that they saturate when the FPGA pin (connected to Base) reads LOW. The Emitter is simply connected to +3.3V. Another thing to clarify is the NPN setup for each row of the keypad (4 row inputs). Following the E155 site instructions, the Emitter was grounded to the FPGA ground, the Base was connected to an FPGA pin (row outputs) via a resistor (\(R_{base}\)). The Collector was wired to the rows of the keypad as shown in ?@fig-schematic and the columns were wired both to the FPGA as column inputs and to +3.3V via a 1 k\(\Omega\) pullup resistor. The value of this resistor is somewhat arbitrary and should be a decent value to pull-up. However, it does inform the value of \(R_{base}\) as stated earlier. The equation is practically \(R_{base} = (3.3V-0.7V)\) where 0.7V is the voltage drop across the resistor divided by \(I_{base}\) which we expect to be \(I_{collector}/10\) or 0.33mA. This ultimately yields a value of 7.8 k\(\Omega\) though a 2.2 k\(\Omega\) serves our purpose of saturating just fine.Results and DiscussionThe overall design and construction was successful as confirmed via simulation (incoming) and through the physical circuitry. I was able to accomplish all tasks outlined in the beginning of this lab report and utilize some interesting code and pin assignment workarounds. Overall, results are as expected and even with a few roadblocks in testbench logic (once again, incoming) and pins being assigned or not reading values. ## Testbench Simulation ::: {.callout-note collapse=“true” title=“View Testbench Simulation”} {#fig-testbench1} ::: The design met all intended design objectives. ?@fig-testbench1 shows a screenshot of the QuestaSim simulation. ::: {.callout-note collapse=“true”} {#fig-testbench2} ::: The design met all intended design objectives. ?@fig-testbench2 shows a screenshot of the QuestaSim simulation. ## Conclusion
The design successfully programmed the 7-segment display and outputted the right LED logic. I learned a lot about testbenches, communication between modules, etc.

text:
In this lab, we once again leveraged the MCU aboard the MicroP’s Dev Board, particularly the STM32L4xx model. The idea was to use interrupts as we make an encoder to tackle measuring the rev/s (and in extension RPM) for a motor going in either direction or having a specified RPM 25GA-370 motor. Interrupts allows us to assess if the encoder functions properly and if the motor skips any pulses because the print logic and direction logic (CW or CCW), illuminates that. With all THESE puzzle pieces, we are able to encode a motor and assess the use of interrupts against other strategies like polling. Additionally, interrupts were actually successful and we know we didn’t skip any pulses because readings would naturally end up randomly switching in direction when no hardware was changed. This was a problem before but quickly patched.
I spent approximately 18 hours in this lab all together including familiarizing myself with the idea and a whole lot of debugging

title: Interrupts
text:
Design and Testing Methodology
Using SEGGER Embedded Studio, the logic of this lab was contained in a header file and a main file.
There are many timers onboard the MCU but TIM2 has 32 bits and is generally recommended so overflow doesn’t occur and we can leverage it’s interrupt as long as pins PA1 and PA2 which also feature IRQHandlers. These are also great because the MCU datasheet states in section 4 Table 14 that these have an I/O Structure of FT_a which is 5V tolerant.
First, data being read out regarding the bits of calculation and the RPS require 1 kHz refresh in the terminal and computing as specified. Since TIM2 was selected, this is 1 ms and with an IRQHandler we can make it so when ARR (aka SAMPL, aka sampling frequency) reaches 999 (and we add 1 in the calculations) it enables an interrupt. This corresponds with 1 second which is what we want. It should even be compatible with the EXTI IRQ Handlers.
The code also notes PPR and is editable to be configured with a motor operating at 150 RPM (408 PPR) though this can be changed. Accounting for the 2 interrupts and the rising and falling edge we don’t just double this. This was an issue but fixed and is now an estimated 1632 counts per revolution.
With all this in mind, to calculate RPS, the formula is RPS = count / (cntsperrev*(SAMPL+1) / 1000). We take into account the timer duration (for that PS of RPS) as well as the expected counts per revolution and count which corresponds to observed pulses in both pins (and rising/falling edges).
To explain better, we can plug in some expected values: Let’s say we put in 10V
Now, an important question to ask is why the need for interrupts. Why would interrupts be better than polling or timers?
Implementing polling would theoretically be far easier than interrupts where we simply read the encoder values as prev, do the calculation and we can do a check to do a calculation every time. Pooling IS simple to integrate but it is set up by counting how many times it reads a value in that 1 second interval. By only relying on digitalRead and timers, we read a value and there is a delay/wait time when a pulse is read. If we’re lucky, it’s fine, but there is a high risk to skip a pulse and be off loop resulting in wildly wrong values or changed in direction where there shouldn’t be. Even if we have a high sampling frequency and low computation, there will still be enough inconsistency for the risk of skipping a pulse to be nonzero.
This also brings up concerns with sampling as a whole with pooling and how some RPS or such can’r be recorded if sampling frequency is not twice or more as the RPS.
Interrupts, theoretically, resolve this because it is not doing the computation all the time and waiting. We only run the computational code when we read soemthing worth processing to trigger an interrupt and thus, processing is more fluid.
In other words, polling has you trapped in a “Data?” while(1) loop which consumes 100% of the CPU’s processing power just for checking. It depends on that loop length for execution and moving on, and it is beholden to the Nyquist Shannon Sampling Theorem.
When implemented, we see the theoretical limitations. For polling, even if we use 80 MHz clock (max for the MCU), our cycles are 12.5 ns and in that time, we have to read the IDR, mask the bit, compare, and then go back in basic assembly. Even with severe optimization, it’s 80 MHz divided by let’s say 5 cycles to do this all. That 16 million polls. In reality, with the printf() and register saving that number goes considerably down. We get an approximate (from experimentation) of 30-50 kHz which is not great.
The limit for an interrupt is latency and the ISR because the NVIC can handle multiple interrupts and neither affects each other. Latency isn’t a concerning issue but the ISR execution time is how much time is spent in the IRQ handlers. If it takes 100 clock cycles (based on code below, that’s more than reasonable) the our limit is 80 MHz/(12+100) or 714 kHz. That is FAR better even in the worst case scenario.
